segments.text: Hello and welcome to this week's Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today, how court actions for deliberately infecting someone with HIV may be affected by changing scientific knowledge.
How Australian research findings have been fast-tracked into clinical practice, potentially helping thousands of pregnant women.
And a leading critic of the current state of medical research argues that big ideas in medical science have become entrenched,
creating fads, and perhaps taking resources from more productive areas.
One of the people arguing this is John Yanidis,
who's Professor in Disease Prevention and Health Research and Policy
at Stanford University in California.
His targets include personalized medicine, stem cell research,
and genetics, particularly genomics.
There are a number of ideas that have dominated biomedical research
and biomedical research funding over the last several decades,

And these include lots of concepts around biology and genetics, genomics in particular, but also any sort of big data and large-scale information where you can combine in-depth knowledge of biology along with in-depth recording of technology and data at high dimensions to try to identify best treatments, best ways to prevent disease, best ways to inform people to do the right things.
and best ways to have people live longer lives.
So this is where most of the funding has gone,
at least in research-savvy communities
that spend tens of billions of dollars in biomedical research.
Apparently, even though these ideas seem to be fascinating,
maybe they haven't really delivered what we have expected them to deliver.
What's your evidence for saying that?
So I think that we need to disentangle the scientific curiosity component,
which is very exciting from what have we learned that can really make a difference in people's
lives and in saving patients or making them live longer and better lives. So genomics and under
genomics one could include not only genetics but maybe any other biological platforms that we can
measure lots of things as well as pharmacogenetics where you try to identify genetic variation that
would tell you which drug is the best to take if you need to take some drug or something else to
treat some disease, plus prevention based on omics, where you use information to make sound
choices about how to prevent disease, and other things like gene therapy, where you try to correct
the genetic effects that underlie disease. So all of these are fascinating ideas. I think we have
learned a lot about the biology, but if you look at how many applications have really moved to the
stage of affecting people's lives and really being documented to be effective and making a difference,
There's very, very few.
The same applies to other technologies in that sphere like stem cell research.
Again, the concept of understanding how stem cells work is a fascinating question from the biology side.
But pretty much the randomized trials that we have done have not really shown any major benefits from stem cell interventions,
much like the clinical trials for gene therapy have not shown much benefit.
So even though the science sounds fascinating and very complex and exciting, we don't have applications that really make a big impact on human health.
So in your analysis, you talk about curiosity-driven research.
You've got all these researchers out there looking at what genes, how they work at the molecular level, talking about precision medicine or personalized medicine, all really hopeful things.
things and you argue in your paper well those ideas have become entrenched and therefore you've
got billions of dollars of almost fixed investment even though it might change between research group
it's a fixed investment almost in those areas what is the problem here is the problem the
curiosity driven research is driven in the wrong direction of curiosity or it's a failure of
implementation based on existing knowledge or we just haven't accepted their dead ends
I'm very much in favor of curiosity-driven research and blue-sky science.
In fact, one of the main problems for these ideas having been entrenched in our research funding universe
is that they do not allow other curiosity-driven research that is even more bold and high-risk
and not within these big domains that are easily recognizable to thrive.
So there's two problems.
One is that we cannot allow to shift the funding to truly high-risk ideas that would explore entirely new concepts,
because there's tens and hundreds of thousands of scientists who are entrenched in these areas,
and they pay off in terms of funding, even though they don't really get very far.
And second, we're not really getting what we thought that these technologies and that type of data and information would deliver.
Precision medicine is probably one of the latest terms to describe.
The same concept that has been out there for many, many years.
And even though there have been a few successes with some information being identifiable that could inform a few people on what is best to do,
these are really the exceptions.
These are really rare exceptions.
In the large scale of things, most people have not really benefited from precision medicine, and I don't think that they will benefit.
By definition, precision medicine is looking at information that each time will benefit very, very few people at the extreme.
it will be just a single person who has a given biological profile,
and then we try to find out what to do with that single person.
But we're talking about a global population of 7 billion,
not easy to catch up just by adding one person at a time.
So you're saying that you're skeptical that precision medicine will ever scale up?
I think it will scale up to some extent,
but it will be nowhere close to catering the needs of population health.
It will probably help hundreds, maybe thousands of people, but not hundreds of millions and billions that we are interested in.
So my question comes back to what I asked you earlier, which is, is this a problem that people call the valley of death?
That we've got all these great ideas coming out of curiosity-driven research and nobody's taking them and applying them?
Or the results of curiosity-driven research are so complicated and dense and difficult that, in fact, it's really an almost impossible task?
We haven't come up with the findings that actually are translatable.
I think it's a combination of both.
There is an issue of complexity and not having easy answers
and also a difficulty in translation and implementation for things that we know
and, you know, if we could get them to work, then they should work.
And one example of that that you use in your paper, sorry to interrupt,
is type 2 diabetes where it was thought that you'd find the genes for type 2 diabetes
but, in fact, it turns out to be a jungle of genes.
Exactly. So I think this is fascinating knowledge.
Personally, I have worked in that space, and some of my most brilliant colleagues have been leaders in that space.
And it's very interesting to find out that there's all these hundreds of genes that may modify by a little bit the risk of getting diabetes.
Now, hopefully we should learn something from these genes, but there are so many and so complex,
And it's very difficult to make real progress and say that we're using this information to eradicate diabetes or even just to diminish diabetes around the world.
So how do you disentangle?
If you say it's both, it's a failure of translation of existing knowledge and that the curiosity-driven research has come up with stuff that you'll never be able to translate.
You know, it's a holistic view of that.
How do you get beyond that?
My suggestion is that we need to invest more on very high risk, innovative, disruptive, out of the box blue sky science.
So instead of just going after that low hanging fruit that seems to be so easy to churn more data and more and more of the same,
I would argue we need to shift a little bit more to allowing ideas that are not within the mainstream to flourish.
You know, the failure rate even for genetics, you know, before the genetic revolution would have been very high.
But nevertheless, we decided to go ahead in that direction.
And we did get some very interesting insights into the genetic architecture.
At least we know that it's very, very complex.
So I think that there's lots of scientists who would be willing to explore high-risk paths if they were supported.
And they didn't have to convince that they just do the type of research that hundreds of thousands of other scientists are doing.
The second component is that we do have a number of things that we have discovered that do seem to work,
and we have identified some major problems that hopefully should be easy to tackle,
and they could translate to saving many millions and potentially billions of lives.
To give you one example, smoking.
We know that smoking is going to kill about a billion people in the next century unless we do something about it.
And we also know that we have effective interventions.
But these interventions do not really depend on complex biology.
They do not depend on complex informational systems.
They're very simple.
Just try to get rid of smoking by increasing taxes, by imposing penalties, by having laws that are pretty strict about advertisement.
But that happens in a different box.
It's a completely different box.
It has no strong biology and no fascinating complexity of biology behind it.
But there are simple tasks and there are simple moves that if we adopt them more globally and more consistently, we can save hundreds of millions of lives.

How do you fix up what you're alleging, which is the groupthink in organizations such as the National Institutes of Health or the National Health and Medical Research Council in Australia or the MRC in the United Kingdom,
which is well recognized, is that you've got an area of research which has forged a path.
They know how to look at it and make assessments of it.
And the people sitting on the committees are doing that research.
So you get this sort of funnel.
And organizations like the Gates Foundation and others have recognized this problem,
which is why they create their challenges.
So you've got the disruptive technology on the side, which loosens up on that.
But the traditional funders who have the billions of dollars in addition to the foundations
have not been very good at that.
I think that one needs some higher level auditing of what's going on.
As you say, some of the most successful scientists are leading these funding institutions.
They're very smart, very successful in what they have done.
But I think that they have a viewpoint that is pretty much stuck to their own universe.
And their universe can only extend that far.
So you need some oversight.

You need someone who would be looking out of the box and be able to tell to these people that this is great, that's wonderful, that we have reached so far and we have learned so much, but we really need to invest also in some avenues that probably will be more productive and would lead eventually to saving more lives for our people in our country and globally.
So I think it's not easy.
I think that the public could play a role.
I think that the public needs to be informed about what we know and what we don't know
and where the biggest gains lie and how could we get there.
Research is wonderful.
I think that investing more in research and in science as a society is one of the best investments,
probably the best investment that a society could aim for.
But at the same time, there's a need to invest on things that could really make a difference
and it would be a pity if we don't do that.
John Ulias, thank you very much for joining us on The Health Report.
Thank you.
John Ulias, who's Professor in Disease Prevention and Health Research and Policy
at Stanford University in California.
You're tuned to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio and CBC Radio across Canada.
I'm Norman Swan.
Listening to that interview with me has been the President of the Australian Society for Medical Research
and testicular physiologist at Monash University, Dr Sarah Meacham.

The ASMR has just released an economic analysis which shows that the current uncertainty and lower success rates of winning research grants is so unsettling scientists that many are thinking of leaving Australia or medical research altogether and that the Australian economy could lose billions of dollars.
Welcome to the Health Report, Sarah.
Thanks, Norman.
So what do you think of Yonidas' point that all of this money is actually going down the tube?
I think what's really important to say on a lot of those points I'm in agreement.
I think the balance of curiosity-driven research to commercialisation is really important,
particularly in Australia as it is in other places around the world.
Australia does very high-quality research and ideas in terms of on a world scale.
However, we are being pushed further and further towards translation and commercialisation outcomes.
In terms of the curiosity-driven research that we do...
I'll just explain, this is where a scientist like you gets an idea and wants to pursue it to test the waters.
And it could be very fundamental research in the laboratory.
Absolutely, very fundamental.
And I think in terms of the curiosity-driven research that we are doing,
because of the very tight funding in Australia.
I think researchers are doing research that is lower in risk
and I think we need to start thinking about pushing things
a little bit like what was discussed before
into more higher risk, blue horizon research.
I think that's absolutely really important
but I don't think that's going to happen
unless we have a secure, sustainable health
and medical research ecosystem in order for researchers to be able to do that.
So in other words, what you're arguing is that as research money becomes tighter,
the agenda becomes tighter too.
Absolutely.
So just very briefly, what are the findings in this research
that you've just done into Australia's medical research community?
I think one of the key findings were is that if we increase investment
investment into the National Health and Medical Research Council to 3% of the health budget,
then the economic benefits of that in terms of health and economic benefits will be over $58
billion over the next 10 years. And I think that's a real goldmine for Australia and national
prosperity. So where do you get that data from, given that we are not very good at translating
our medical research findings into action.
You quote fact figures of a return of, say, $9.80 per dollar
invested in cardiovascular research and $3.70 in cancer research.
Where's that coming from, that money?
Well, it's coming from numerous places,
obviously from the commercialisation and marketplace end.
I mean, Australia, even though we don't commercialise
as well as other countries, we are still commercialising
and we do have fantastic ideas that do also go abroad.
And think of also the big biotechs.
For example, in Australia, like ResMed and CSL,
they bring an enormous amount of money back to the Australian economy.
And you argue that the...
And sorry, what percentage of the health budget is it at the moment?
You say you argue for 3%?
Yeah, it's 0.55% at the moment.
So it's got to go up by a lot.
Absolutely.
So what would be the total research budget of the National Health and Medical Research Council if they got 3%?
If we got 3%, it would be in the order of $5.4 billion in 2025.
At the moment, we're looking at $0.8 billion.
But according to your report, we won't have any researchers left to actually use that money.
Well, that's quite a concern and that's why we're talking about it today.
Over three years, we've had a loss of in order of 15% of our expert workforce.
And that's a hell of a lot for three years.
And we're really just at the tip of the iceberg.
If there's no further investment over the next few years,
that number is going to increase dramatically.
Sarah Meacham, thanks for joining us.
Welcome.
Sarah Meacham, who's president of the Australian Society for Medical Research
and a medical researcher herself.
Well, just to show that some Australian research can
and does make it into the clinic to help people,
there's news that a test for a common problem in pregnancy is now being used,
even though the definitive paper showing that it works was only published a few months ago.
The condition is called preeclampsia, where a pregnant woman has high blood pressure,
fluid retention, often with swollen ankles, and signs of kidney damage with protein in the urine.
The risk is injury or even death to the baby, and a condition called eclampsia,
which can cause stroke in the mother and indeed death.
In our Melbourne studio is Professor Sean Brennecke,
who's Director of the Department of Perinatal Medicine
and Head of the Pregnancy Research Centre at the Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne.
Welcome to The Health Report.
Thank you, Norman.
Why do you need a test when it's obvious when a woman's got preeclampsia, isn't it?
She's got high blood pressure, she's got protein in her urine, she's got fluid.
Well, once she has preeclampsia, yes, the diagnosis is obvious,
but the issue really is how do you detect the woman who is showing some early signs of what might be preeclampsia
but often does not turn out to be preeclampsia, and that's where this new test is proving its value.
And what sort of, just describe a woman in that situation,
where she might have a bit of blood pressure or something like that?
Yes, she might have some temporary increases in blood pressure.
She might have some excessive swelling.
She might have some symptoms such as a headache.
All of these things are relatively common in many women during pregnancy,
and the majority of them do not turn out to have full-blown preeclampsia.

So the ability to distinguish between those who will develop preeclampsia and those who do not have a high chance of developing preeclampsia is a very important step in our diagnostic evaluation during pregnancy.
So what's this test?
Well, it goes by an unusual name.
It's called an SFLIT1 PLGF ratio.
It's got that ring to it, the sort of marketing ring.
Somebody's really thought hard about this.
Yes.
The test is made up of two proteins that are released from the placenta during pregnancy
into the mother's blood circulation.
S-Flit1 is one protein and PLGF is the other protein.
The interesting thing about these two proteins is that one of them goes up and the other
one goes down in women destined to develop preeclampsia.
In particular, the S-Flit1 goes up and the PLGF goes down.
Is this because the placenta is the source of preeclampsia?
That's correct.
The current understanding is that the organ responsible for preeclampsia is the placenta.
And that is why the only cure for preeclampsia at the end of the day is delivery of the mother of her baby and the placenta.
So what happens to the S-flit and P1GF in S-flit 1, I should say, and PLGF when a woman is developing preeclampsia?
The S-Flit1 goes up and the PLGF goes down some weeks before the clinical diagnosis of preeclampsia is possible.
And given that one of the proteins, S-Flit1, goes up and the other one, PLGF, goes down,
by creating a ratio of S-Flit1 over PLGF, that provides an excellent discrimination.
It empowers the test to a greater degree than using either protein on its own
so that you have a better ability early on before the clinical syndrome is present to the clinician to make the call.
So I'm told that this is actually better not for diagnosing preeclampsia,
but for actually telling women they don't have it.
That's true.
In the study that was published earlier this year in the New England Journal of Medicine,
the so-called negative predictive value of this test,
that is the ability to exclude the development of preeclampsia was almost 98%.
In contrast to that, the ability to predict precisely who would develop preeclampsia
was much lower at about 40%.
So what are the chances then that a woman's told you're definitely not going to get preeclampsia
because we've done this wonderful new test?
What are the chances are that they got that wrong?
It's a bit complicated when you talk about these predictive values.
That's right.
Over a four-week period, it would be about 5% error rate.
So what happens to that 5% where you've got it wrong?
Well, in fact, during a normal supervision of a pregnancy,
most women would be attending, particularly in the latter half of pregnancy,
on a fortnightly or weekly basis.
so you would still have supervision of those women in the antenatal clinic.
The important thing about the women with suspected preeclampsia in the past
is that they've often had to be admitted to hospital
for the detailed supervision that was required
and that's quite expensive from a health economics point of view
and also quite disruptive to the woman's own domestic circumstances.

So if you're able on an outpatient basis to, on a weekly or fortnightly basis, predict that a woman isn't going to develop preeclampsia, that can be a very helpful test both for the mother in terms of her domestic circumstances and also for the health economics of pregnancy care.
But if you're still going to have to monitor them quite intensively, what benefit have you actually got?
Because you've got to watch out for that 5% who can get into strife.
It's the degree of intensity.
On the one hand, outpatient visits would be considered less intensive.
And on the other hand, if you have to admit women to hospital to do that surveillance,
that's quite expensive.
And I think this test is well placed to allow you to monitor the vast majority of women
on an outpatient basis without having to admit them to hospital for the surveillance that
would otherwise have been necessary with the old-fashioned testing.
And while I lauded the fact that it was being put into action, it's really only the Royal
Women's in Australia that's doing it.
Within Australia at the moment, that's correct as I understand it.
However, in a number of centres overseas, particularly in Europe, the test is underway as well.
So, yes, more interested in Australia.
Have you managed to convince your colleagues to use it?
Well, we're in the process of doing that, and I'm trusting that radio interviewers like this might facilitate that.
Might convince the Sydney operators and the Brisbane operators that they can do it.
Thank you very much, Sean.
My pleasure.
Sean, just before we get him into trouble with his colleagues
Sean Brenneke is Director of the Department of Perinatal Medicine
and the Head of the Pregnancy Research Centre at Royal Women's Hospital in Melbourne
A paper published today in the Medical Journal of Australia
argues that the criminal justice system in Australia
should be very careful about prosecuting cases
alleging deliberate transmission of HIV
The science and treatment have moved on to such an extent
that the risk of sexual transmission has become much lower
says the paper
The lead author is Mark Boyd
who's Professor of Medicine at the University of Adelaide
welcome to the health report. Thanks for the invitation Norman. So what's the typical story
here? Look yeah let me answer you in general terms Norman because it's certainly not our
intention of the authors or of the statement to directly critique the evidence presented in the
past in such cases in the trials or to suggest a miscarriage of justice in any of those trials.
But having said that in general terms what we're addressing in the statement are court cases in
which there is an accusation by one individual that another person, the defendant, has deliberately
infected the complainant with HIV infection and had not disclosed before engaging in sex
their HIV status and had not taken adequate precautions to minimise the risk of transmission.
Are there still many of those cases around? It used to be a few, but are there still many around?
There aren't that many.
Look, overall, in the 30-odd years since the epidemic, you know,
was first called, I guess, in the early 80s,
there's been about 40, I think 38 cases overall in Australia,
and they still do occur.
So tell us what...
I mean, you're trying to say here that the evidentiary position
has changed over the years and the law needs to catch up a bit.
That's absolutely right.
I think, you know, our intention really was to, in a sense,
bring the ever-evolving science of HIV, and it is a field in which science, clinical science
and basic science moves incredibly rapidly, to try and appraise the criminal justice system
of the situation with HIV at the present time. And I think there are two important aspects that
we want to highlight. One is that in previous times, the notion that someone became infected
with HIV was essentially thought of as, you know, inverted commas, a death sentence. You know, it was
a heinous illness which would shorten people's lives substantially and may well lead to a fairly
unpleasant death, you know, as a result of immunodeficiency. And in the past 20 years,
particularly in 20 to 30 years, where there's been an enormous effort to try and treat HIV,
we've now got to a situation in which the great majority of people infected with HIV,
particularly in a country like Australia, where there's a universal healthcare system and access
to therapy. Most of those people are now seen as outpatients lead extremely healthy and productive
lives. And we believe, and there's certainly plenty of evidence now that they really could
be expected to live the same kind of life in terms of flight and duration.
So that argument goes to damages, if you like.
Indeed. So it's now no longer such a terrible diagnosis. It's completely compatible with a
reasonable life if you simply... And we've now got a range of tablets.
Well, it's still a pretty rotten thing to deliberately infect somebody if you know that you've got it and you haven't taken precautions.
Absolutely.
That's quite true.
But I think what's important is that it's quite unusual to have cases in which people have deliberately gone out and infected people.
These are very unusual cases.
The great majority of transmissions are simply unfortunate and a bit of an accident.
So then you go to the science of transmission.
Right.

So in that regard, we've also got a much better handle, I think, now on the sort of risk of transmission for any given act for a person with HIV infection, whether they've been on treatment or not, and whether they're using barrier protection, for instance, condoms or not.
And you argue that the risk these days is incredibly low for sexual transmission.
It is incredibly low, yeah.
Yeah, and in fact, there've been some really fantastic studies that have been published
only in the recent past.
And this has all come out of an understanding that we probably needed to find other tools
other than condoms, whether they be male condoms or female condoms, to try and limit
transmission even more.
So in the last five to six years, we've seen studies, very good, robust, randomized clinical
trials that have demonstrated if you give people prophylaxis, so using a component of
that combination antiretroviral therapy, which can be taken at one pill daily.
and that person takes that pill daily,
then the chances of transmission to that person,
even if they're exposed to someone with HIV,
with whatever viral load you like,
so quite high levels of HIV in the body, is pretty much zero.
So you're arguing that because of this, we're almost running out of time,
but you're arguing because of this,
that in fact many of these cases should not go to trial
because, i.e., the risks are low
and maybe a public health approach is a more appropriate way to go.
Absolutely.
I mean, we think that the public health approach can be adapted to these people, people who are even deliberately infecting people.
It's much better to try and treat them with a public health framework in which they can be counselled and followed up and, you know, if necessary, isolators.
But we don't believe that necessarily incarceration and criminal prosecution is appropriate.
It's not good for the individual and it probably doesn't improve the public health.
And the burden of proof for lawyers is going to get much higher, is much higher than it used to be.
Yes, we believe so.
Thank you very much indeed, Mark Boyd, for joining us.
That's a pleasure.
Mark Boyd is Professor of Medicine at the University of Adelaide.
I'm Norman Swan, and this has been The Health Report.
I hope you can join me next week.
